title: Differential pair DC bias and large-signal behavior

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
The source-coupled pair's large-signal behaviour follows from two facts. Each device obeys the square law, and the tail fixes \(I_{D1} + I_{D2} = I_{SS}\). At balance each carries \(I_{SS}/2\) at overdrive \(V_{ov}\). As the differential input \(v_{id}\) grows, current shifts toward one side. The difference \(I_{D1} - I_{D2}\) rises linearly at first, with slope \(g_m = I_{SS}/V_{ov}\), then bends over. When \(|v_{id}| = \sqrt2V_{ov}\) one device turns off and the other carries everything. Larger overdrive means a wider linear range but less \(g_m\).

The DC bias sets the **input common-mode range**. The lowest common-mode voltage must leave enough voltage across the tail source: \(V_{CM} \ge V_{GS} + V_{tail,\min}\). The highest must keep the input devices saturated: their drains, at \(V_{DD} - I_{SS}R_D/2\), must stay above \(V_{CM} - V_T\). Inside that window the pair behaves as a linear differential amplifier.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ I_{D1} - I_{D2} = \tfrac12kv_{id}\sqrt{\frac{4I_{SS}}{k} - v_{id}^2}, \quad k = \mu_nC_{ox}\tfrac WL, \qquad |v_{id}|_{\max} = \sqrt2V_{ov} \]
\[ V_{GS} + V_{tail,\min} \le V_{CM} \le V_{DD} - \tfrac12I_{SS}R_D + V_T \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A pair with \(I_{SS} = 1\ \mathrm{mA}\) and \(k = 4\ \mathrm{mA/V^2}\) balances at \(V_{ov} = \sqrt{1/4} = 0.5\ \mathrm{V}\), so it fully steers at 0.71 V and has \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\). With \(V_T = 0.38\ \mathrm{V}\), a 0.22 V tail minimum, \(R_D = 1.5\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and a 3.3 V supply, the common-mode window runs from 1.10 V to 2.93 V.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Computing \(g_m\) with the full tail current instead of half.
- Forgetting the tail source's own headroom in the lower CM limit.
- Extrapolating the linear gain past the steering limit.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Inside the linear window, small-signal analysis by half circuits takes over; a finite tail resistance leads to common-mode gain.
